newsitem.title: UK: European copper tight but scrap may filter through.
newsitem.headline: European copper tight but scrap may filter through.

text.p: The European copper market is still tight with London Metal Exchange (LME) stocks depleted, consumption picking up and scrap material being withheld.
But scrap merchants are expected to be more willing sellers following this month's sharp rise in copper prices, helping to ease the situation, traders, merchants and producers said.
"Copper in Europe is still very tight," a merchant said.
"Scrap and Russian metal is tight, LME stocks are low and some very difficult to get hold of," another added.
The shortage of scrap resulted from the steep price fall in May and June which left merchants holding loss-making metal.

According to analysts, scrap accounts for 30 to 35 percent of total copper supply. Consumers have had to take more Russian copper to substitute low scrap availability, and lately more LME-deliverable metal to substitute low Russian supplies. "We expect to see more scrap come into the market. At $2,200 (on a three months basis) we will definitely see more material," said a producer source.

"Initially you could get a good spurt of scrap coming out," a physical trader added. But scrap dealers suggested the flow would be slower. "Obviously the higher prices go the more attractive scrap will be and the more efficient people will get. But I don't think it will happen immediately," said one scrap trader.
He added that scrap prices have not risen as sharply as primary values, increasing merchants' reluctance to sell.
Traders said demand for copper was picking up in Europe, although the region still lagged the Far East and U.S.
"There has been a little bit of a consumer pick-up Europe-wide," said a merchant.

Producers were still actively switching material in November by buying copper from LME warehouses and shipping it to the Far East. But the arbitrage "window" had almost closed following the rise in European premiums.
"Premiums in Europe are going up and we won't be able to ship to Asia forever. We are already very close to the limit," said one producer.
Producers have also been offering to buy back material destined for European end-users to switch to Asia, but consumers were generally reluctant to do so, suggesting end-user stocks were tight.
"There are no clients in Europe cancelling. They obviously need the copper because they have the option of receiving good premiums for the material instead," the producer added.
Traders said the slowdown in the rate of LME stock declines was likely to continue, and inventories may even start to build during December as more copper is delivered into the Singapore warehouse.
But some said the amount of material available for re-export from China was lower than originally expected.
"I understand that they (China's state reserve) have custom cleared most of the material that has gone out there," a senior trader said last week, estimating the total at 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes.
The market was expected to remain tight during December, and further price spikes should be expected, some traders said.
Spot premiums were quoted flat to slightly higher than late-October levels, although traders said some differentials were notional with material so tight.
Russian copper was traded at a $10-a-tonne discount to LME cash for delivery in December.
